Annex five also encourages the secretariat, financial institutions and relevant partners to identify and mobilize dedicated resources to ensure the sustainability, effectiveness and wider uptake of these platforms across regions. The group's countries have made significant progress in developing their accounting monitoring system as part of preparations for the fourth PRA cycle. We would note that the reporting process highlighted not only merits and advantages, but also systemic problems which require joint solutions. For example, The first problem is the discrepancy between the global indicators and the national land-based data. We saw that trends earth or other global products did not distinguish, between secondary salination of lands. They didn't reflect, they didn't distinguish between healthy pasture land from degraded, where valuable cereals are replaced with wormwood or non-palatable species. This so-called green desertification, where the green color on satellite images seems to show that everything's okay, but in fact, it means that that's not by any means the case. Therefore, what logically what we need is a blended approach, global remote data as a basis, but with pre-training for the model using ground-based observation, countries in the region are ready to provide their many years of soil, geo-botanical and agrochemical surveys, we call on the secretariat, FAO, UNDP and UNEP to create a regional verification hub where such national data can be fine-tuned and integrated into global reporting. Now the second problem is fragmentation of departmental data. Now, this is probably a problem in many countries and our country is no exception. We have the land cadastre, the agrochemical service, the forest registry, water management department. Often there are parallel information systems and it leads to duplications, contradictions and multiple manual entry and re-entry of the same indicators into PRACE 4. Now, our proposal is to develop a national single platform for data on land degradation with integration of all specialized agencies. Kazakhstan, for example, has already created its own digital land resource platform. Uzbekistan is establishing its own national forest and pasture monitoring system. Kyrgyzstan land map of resources and so there have been good examples also in Turkmenistan, in Tajikistan also. In Russia, powerful scientific basis exists to develop such data and coordinating such data. Now a third problem is a lack of qualified specialists and the complexity of the price for interface. Now many specialists on the ground aren't that familiar with GIS and with remote sounding. The price for interface notwithstanding all its merits is still difficult to use. And so we're calling the secretariat and donors to maybe organize a series of regional workshops in the local languages on how to work with PRAIS4, Trends Earth and ground-based verification systems. We also support introduction of a easy user friendly mobile interface to collect data. in situ. A fourth problem is a limited reflection of national indicators. The global methodology doesn't always reflect our own specific processes when it comes to salination, wind erosion, shifting sands or mountain pasture degradation. So we propose supplementing the mandatory three global indicators with optional national indicators, for example, using spectrum analysis of salination, grass species composition, and also fixed sands, surface area of fixed sands. countries in the region are ready to present their methodology and pilot results we call on the convention secretariat to include in the reporting manual a section on using national indicators as baselines. Colleagues, reporting should be an important practical guidance instrument that is why we call to introduce a multi-level system of oversight verification of data with the participation of states, but also independent experts and local communities. We urge the CRIC to recommend to COP17 the following solutions. First of all, consolidate a combined approach using global and national data as the standard. to direct the secretariat together with its partners to develop a technical assistance program on creating national integrated data platforms for the Central Asia countries. Thirdly, organize regional workshops on price for GIS and remote monitoring with translation of materials into Russian and in the national languages. Fourth, encourage use of additional national indicators, creating a repository for them within the CCD website. And here at our COP 17, this has already been raised, the use of AI. Since we are in the business of land, water, making ecosystems more healthy, we should point out that using AI might not be such a bad thing. It's, it's so, you know, it might affect farmers. So when it comes to using AI, we need to know the risks and we, and sufficiently upstream properly regulate AI for using artificial intelligence. Thank you.

Thank you, Chair. My name is Fauzia Noor. I'll be delivering the statement on behalf of civil societies. Distinguished delegates, we appreciate the GRIIC's effort to strengthen accountability, monitor progress, and support UNCCD implementation. However, success must be measured not only by policies, reports, and strategies, but by results on the ground, like restored ecosystem, resilient livelihoods, empowered communities, fulfilled human rights and improved living conditions. We call on parties on six key priorities. First is to strengthen community-centered implementation. National action programs and land degradation neutrality targets must ensure meaningful, structured, and inclusive participation through planning, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation. Communities are partners, knowledge holders, land stewards, innovators, and implementers, and therefore they should be included in decision making. Second, transform capacity building into long-term empowerment. Investment must support local leadership and governance systems. It also must integrate indigenous traditional knowledge, youth innovation, and gender transformative action. Capacity building must also recognize and elevate knowledge generated and handled by communities themselves. Third, We also call upon the improve of local access to implementation resources. We urge parties and relevant institutions to create more inclusive financing pathways while realizing the rights of communities to pursue their own self-determined economies. Fourth, strengthen regional cooperation and knowledge exchange. Land degradation and droughts cross borders. Regional platforms should promote cooperation, knowledge exchange and partnerships on agroecology, restoration, scientific and indigenous practices, local solution, ensuring vulnerable regions shape global implementation. Fifth, strengthen accountability and transparency. Monitoring must ensure social outcomes alongside quantitative indicators, including resilience, equality, participation. Lastly, we call for more funding to reach local communities. We are concerned that environmental funding is declining. Parties must commit at the highest level to increase funding and make it directly accessible to local communities and also organizations. Excellencies, our message is clear, restore the land, but also restore the voices of the people who protect the land. Let COP17 put communities and local solutions at the heart of implementation. Thank you.

Thank you, Madam Chair, and good afternoon, distinguished delegates. I am very pleased to present to you some key points of the UNCCD work plan for the next year. and the document on the performance of the Secretariat and the Global Mechanism in the biennium 2025-2026. But before going to the content, let me present some matters concerning the documentation and the organization of work. The Secretariat has, for the first time, submitted to this COP an integrated programme budget. In other words, the budget document now contains also the main content of the work plan, including an indication of the cost of the achievement of the expected results. Unlike in earlier years, we have not prepared a separate document for the work plan to avoid duplication. Nevertheless, in line with the terms of reference of the CRIC, We continue informing the CRIC of the work plan and performance of the Secretariat and the GM as has been done earlier. They are an important component to the consideration of the overall performance of the UNCCD, which is the main task of the CRIC. As usual, the results presented by the Secretariat would be considered at the Budget Contact Group, which is convened under the Committee of the Whole. Now, I would like to move to the content. So let's start with the performance highlights as presented in document ICCD COP 17 INF 4. That document shows that in the 2025-2026 biennium, the Secretariat and the GM managed to achieve important results in terms of advancing cooperation and partnerships for implementation, involving new stakeholders and gaining media attention among other things. To mention just a few examples, LDN is advancing. 116 countries, which is basically two thirds of countries of the world, have completed their national voluntary land degradation neutrality targets. 22 projects to implement action toward those targets, which were prepared with support from the GM, were approved for implementation. The total financing of these projects is approximately $1.48 billion. Another example, the ecological, economic, and social value of rangelands is increasingly recognized. One major contributor for that has been the Silk Road Caravan that has reached at least 200 million people online. Partnerships that will provide effective means to implement proactive measures for drought resilience building are starting to be in place, including the International Drought Resilience Alliance, the Riyadh Global Drought Resilience Partnership, the International Drought Resilience Observatory, and most recently, the Drought Resilience Investment Facility. We are witnessing a massive rise in the involvement of non-governmental stakeholders. Over 300 private sector entities are registered to the Business for Land process, including some major global companies. The lodging of the caucus of indigenous peoples, the caucus for local communities, is well underway. The number of non-state actor applications that applied for accreditation to the COP is growing fast. For COP16, we received 437 applications, while for COP17, we had already in June more than 890 applications. These were just a few examples of the concrete achievements that we have delivered jointly in the last years. The 2025-2026 biennium has not been marked only by many major achievements. The Secretariat and the GM have also had to deal with an increasing uncertainty of the ability to continue delivering important achievements due to the unexpected shortfall of core budget contributions and the resulting decline in some key human resources. Out of the 45 staff that we have under the core budget, the Secretariat and the GM have had to freeze five to avoid overspending their resources. This has taken a heavy toll on the UNCCD staff that has remained. many of whom have assumed duties that go far beyond their job description and exceed any normal working hours. This is not a sustainable approach. Now, let's have a look at what we are planning for the coming years. The Secretariat and the GM propose a work program for 2027-2028 that combines targeted action with enhanced efficiency. Priorities remain focused on the interlinked agendas of land and drought, brought forward through expanding stakeholder involvement and increased organizational effectiveness. Securing soil health for the production of adequate and affordable food and for a variety of industries is a defining priority that shapes efforts for protecting and restoring land. We hope to further advance measures and collaboration to protect and restore rangelands and to maintain and improve the productivity of agricultural lands. LDN remains the key tool for the implementation of the Convention and integrated land use planning in refining and preparing the LDN targets will support the use of various measures within a comprehensive coordinated framework. No lives should be lost to drought in the 21st century and the UNCCD is the prime tool for advancing that aim. We plan to continue bringing forth the partnerships and other forms of support that will enable countries to implement effective, proactive measures for addressing drought. Meeting the UNCCD aims for land and drought mitigation cannot be done via public funding and government actions only. Other stakeholders will need to take an active role as well. For 2027, 2028, the Secretariat and the GM are proposing measures and collaboration to strengthen private sector engagement from two perspectives. First, making it easier for private companies to invest in protecting land and mitigating drought impact by reducing investment risks, and two, advancing policies that prevent or reduce unsustainable approaches. The involvement of other key stakeholders, including women, youth, civil society organizations, local communities, and indigenous peoples will be facilitated. And lastly, we will continue enhancing the efficiency of our own institutional performance in 2027, 2028, recognizing that the global economic situation is likely to hinder the availability of additional resources. Particular attention will be placed on exploring the potential of further digitalization of our key processes and using artificial intelligence. Thank you for your attention.
